title: How To Create A Zen-Like Classroom In One Minute minute/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes how a teacher's own harried energy on a rushed morning can transfer directly to students, producing an excitable, tension-filled classroom that invites misbehavior. As an antidote, he presents the 'one minute of silence' strategy: on a signal, students sit silently and focus on slow, deep breathing for sixty seconds while the teacher models calm by sitting still and breathing along with them rather than using the time to get tasks done. He explains the physiological logic — slow breathing lowers heart rate and blood pressure, calming both body and mind — and offers guidance for restarting the timer if a student talks or fidgets. He recommends using the strategy multiple times a day as maintenance, before important assignments, or as a calming close to the school day, framing it as a way to release built-up tension before it turns into misbehavior.
points: A teacher's own rushed, excitable energy transfers directly to students and raises classroom tension.
The 'one minute of silence' strategy uses slow, deep breathing to lower physiological arousal for both students and teacher.
The teacher must model stillness during the minute rather than using it to get other tasks done, since students emulate the teacher's energy.
The strategy can be used proactively (before tests, before recess) or as maintenance several times a day to prevent excitability from building.
quotes: Your students pick up on your nervous energy and they too become excitable. Heads swivel left and right, voices carry and bounce around the room, and the clatter and clang of an overactive classroom becomes a major annoyance.
Whatever the cause, excitable students and tension-filled classrooms encourage misbehavior and make classroom management a far greater challenge.

It’s important, however, that you don’t move around the classroom and try to get things done. Your students will emulate the energy you give off, and if you’re stressed and buzzing about, they will respond in kind.

The reason slow breathing works is because it lowers the heart rate and blood pressure, calming both the body and the mind. It is said that one cannot become stressed or nervous if the body remains perfectly relaxed.
Using the one minute of silence strategy is like opening a valve on a pressure cooker, releasing nervous energy, tension, and excitability from your classroom.
